summary.text: Instinct is the inherent inclination of a living organism towards a particular complex behaviour that contains innate, inborn elements.
A behaviour is instinctive if it is performed without prior experience, and the simplest example is a fixed action pattern.
Newly hatched sea turtles move toward the ocean by instinct, and a newborn marsupial climbs into its mother's pouch.

facts.label: Versus reflexes
facts.value: Instincts are complex; reflexes are simple responses

facts.label: Maslow's view
facts.value: Humans can override urges, so lack instincts

items.prompt: Newly hatched turtles scurry toward the sea on a beach they have never seen. Why can they do this?

options.label: An inborn response that needs no prior experience
They were taught the route by older turtles
They worked it out by trial and error that morning
They copied the first turtle to move

items.explain: A behaviour is instinctive if it is performed without prior experience, as an expression of innate biological factors.

items.prompt: A doctor taps a patient's knee and the lower leg jerks. How does this differ from a bird building a nest?

options.label: The jerk is a learned habit, while nest building is a simple response
Both are reflexes, though nest building simply takes longer
The jerk is a simple response; nest building is a complex inborn pattern
The jerk is an instinct, while nest building is a reflex

items.explain: Instincts are inborn complex patterns of behaviour, which should be distinguished from reflexes, the simple responses to a specific stimulus such as the knee jerk.

items.prompt: A bird builds nests the same way every year but gets smoother at it with practice. Does that mean nest building is not an instinct?

options.label: Yes; any change from practice shows a behaviour is learned
No; experience can change details of the performance while the behaviour stays innate
Yes; instincts must be performed identically every time
No; practice turns the behaviour into a reflex

items.explain: An instinct is defined by its invariant innate characteristics, but details of its performance can be changed by experience.

items.prompt: A researcher interrupts several wasp species mid-hunt, and nearly all keep repeating the same steps anyway. Which conclusion matches Fabre's?

options.label: Wasps reason through each hunt as it comes
Wasps adjust their behaviour within minutes of the interruption
Instincts change quickly because species evolve into one another
Instincts are fixed patterns, and animals cannot reason around them

items.explain: Fabre saw most species keep their fixed pattern when he intervened, and concluded instincts are fixed and that most animals cannot reason.

items.prompt: Wundt studied how babies' faces react to sweet, sour and bitter tastes. How did he explain where instincts come from?

options.label: Each baby learns them within its first weeks
Natural selection caused small changes in the nervous system over time
They come from mental images of bodily needs
They are overridden once consciousness develops

items.explain: Wundt explained instincts through natural selection, which causes small changes in the nervous system over time and brings about hereditary drives.

items.prompt: Someone talks themselves out of a strong urge. On Maslow's view, what does this show?

options.label: It was a drive, not an instinct, because instincts cannot be overridden
It was an instinct that Freud's death drive caused
It was a reflex like the knee jerk
It shows humans have stronger instincts than animals

items.explain: Maslow argued that an instinct cannot be overridden, so what people call instinct is really strong drives.

paragraphs.heading: What an instinct is
paragraphs.text: An instinct is a built-in leaning of a living thing toward a particular complex behaviour, with parts that are present from birth. A behaviour counts as instinctive when it is done without relying on earlier experience, that is, without learning, so it expresses innate biology. Every animal has instincts, humans included. They are complex inborn patterns shared by most members of a species.

paragraphs.heading: Instincts and reflexes
paragraphs.text: Instincts should be kept apart from reflexes, which are simple responses to one specific trigger, like the pupil narrowing in bright light or the lower leg jerking when the knee is tapped. The simplest kind of instinct is a fixed action pattern: a short to medium run of actions, done without variation, set off by a clearly defined trigger, or stimulus. Even so, experience can adjust how an instinct is carried out. A dog, for instance, can get better at listening through practice.

paragraphs.heading: Instincts in action
paragraphs.text: Newly hatched sea turtles head for the ocean without having learned to. A newborn marsupial climbs into its mother's pouch. Fighting, courtship, nest building and internal escape functions are other examples. People can sometimes halt a fixed action pattern by noticing the moment it is set off and simply stopping, whereas animals with too little will power may be unable to break off once it has started.

paragraphs.heading: Fabre and the wasps
paragraphs.text: Jean Henri Fabre (1823–1915) specialized in the instincts of insects. He saw an instinct as a linked chain of behaviours that an animal carries out unconsciously in response to its surroundings, and he believed these chains were fixed, not changing when the situation was new. His study of several wasp species shaped this view. Each species followed a set routine when catching prey, but when Fabre interfered with the capture, only one species changed what it did. He treated individuals that departed from their species' norm as exceptions, while granting that instincts might have some room to grow.

paragraphs.heading: Fixed patterns and reason
paragraphs.text: Fabre watched insects and wild birds keep repeating a behaviour in a new situation, even when it did not help them. From this he concluded that most animals, unlike humans, cannot reason, and that this is a key difference between them. His belief that instincts are fixed runs against the theory of evolution. He rejected the idea that one species could turn into another, and that human consciousness could arise from the evolution of unconscious traits.

paragraphs.heading: Wundt and natural selection
paragraphs.text: In 1879, at the University of Leipzig, Wilhelm Wundt (1832–1920) set up the first psychology laboratory. He thought unconscious processes, which he called instinctive movements, came from sensations and emotions and were building blocks of consciousness. He watched the faces babies made when tasting sweet, sour and bitter things, and decided the expressions were attempts to avoid unpleasant feelings from something in the mouth. In his account, such instincts became innate because earlier generations learned them and they aided survival. He explained this through natural selection, which slowly alters the nervous system and gives rise to inherited drives.

paragraphs.heading: Do people have instincts
paragraphs.text: Sigmund Freud described instincts as biological forces that push people to meet their needs, and split them into life instincts (Eros), tied to survival, reproduction and pleasure, and death instincts (Thanatos), tied to aggression and self-destruction. William McDougall linked many instincts to particular emotions. As research grew more rigorous, instinct became a less common way to explain human behaviour. In 1932 McDougall suggested keeping the word for animals and using propensity for flexible blends of innate human abilities. In the 1950s Abraham Maslow said humans no longer have instincts, since people can override them in some situations and, for him, a true instinct cannot be overridden.
